igcse-0580-practical-graphs-conversion.description: Read axes and scales, plot data and use a straight graph to convert in either direction.

sections.title: How do I read from the horizontal axis?
sections.label: From input
sections.intro: Read what both axes measure. Find the given input on the horizontal scale, then go up to the line and across to the other scale.

blocks.html: Choose scales that fit all the data. Label both axes with their units. Use a straight line when the quantities are related by a constant scale factor.

figure.alt: A straight conversion line from zero through nine and 27.
figure.caption: The line represents 3 grams per card. Read the matching coordinate using the two labelled scales.

blocks.prompt:
Cards printedPaper used (g)
00
12132
24264
36396

A printer uses paper at a fixed rate. The table lists points on a straight conversion graph. How many grams are needed for 25 cards?
blocks.hint: Identify the scale factor from a table row or use the straight line between marked points.
blocks.solution:
The rate is \(132\div 12=11\) g per card.

Read the line above 25 cards. The corresponding reading is \(25\times 11\) g.

The answer is \(275\).

blocks.solution:

Read the line above 33 cards. The corresponding reading is \(33\times 4\) g.

The answer is \(132\).

sections.title: How do I read in the opposite direction?
sections.label: From output
sections.intro: If the known value belongs to the vertical axis, start on that axis. Go across to the line, then down.

blocks.html: Start on the axis that measures the given quantity.

blocks.hint: Start at the known measurement on its labelled axis. Read from the other axis.
blocks.solution:
One card uses 12 g. On the graph, start from 324 on the vertical scale.

Go across to the line, then down to the horizontal scale.

The answer is \(27\).

sections.title: What if the line does not start at zero?
sections.label: Starting fee
sections.intro: A cost graph might start at a fixed fee. Its height tells you the total cost and its gradient tells you the extra cost for one unit.

blocks.html: Use differences between two points to work out a rate of change.

blocks.prompt:
ItemsTotal price (£)
015
1485
28155

These points lie on a straight cost graph. What is the cost per extra item, in pounds?

field.label: Cost in pounds per extra item

blocks.hint: Use differences between two points. The graph may start above zero.
blocks.solution:
The cost rises by 70 pounds when the item count rises by 14.

Divide the rise in cost by the rise in items: \(70\div 14\).

The answer is \(5\).

igcse-0580-practical-graphs-distance.description: Read a distance from home, find stops and work out speed for one segment or an entire journey.

sections.title: What does a flat segment mean?
sections.label: Stop
sections.intro: Check what the vertical axis measures. When the distance from home stays the same along a flat straight segment, the journey graph describes a stop.

blocks.html: Subtract the starting time of the flat segment from its ending time.

figure.alt: Distance from home rises, stays level, then returns to zero.
figure.caption: The flat segment shows a stop. The final segment returns the traveller to the starting place.

blocks.prompt:
Time from start (min)Distance from home (m)
00
1442
1942
250

The times are marked on a piecewise straight journey graph. How many minutes does Ali stay still?
blocks.hint: A flat distance graph means the person is not moving.
blocks.solution:
The distance reading is unchanged between 14 and 19 minutes.

Subtract the start of the flat section from its end.

The answer is \(5\).

blocks.html: A horizontal line on a speed–time graph means something different.

blocks.prompt:
Time from start (min)Distance from home (m)
00

The times are marked on a piecewise straight journey graph. How many minutes does Ali stay still?
blocks.hint: A flat distance graph means the person is not moving.
blocks.solution:
The distance reading is unchanged between 7 and 16 minutes.

Subtract the start of the flat section from its end.

The answer is \(9\).

sections.title: What does a falling distance from home show?
sections.label: Return
sections.intro: A straight downward segment shows distance from the start decreasing steadily. The traveller is returning towards home.

blocks.html: Use the absolute change in distance from home and divide by the elapsed time on that part.

blocks.prompt:
Time from start (min)Distance from home (m)
00
1560
2160
280

The table gives the vertices of a distance–time graph. What is the speed on the final segment, in metres per minute? Give your answer exactly.
blocks.hint: A negative gradient shows direction towards home. Speed is non-negative.
blocks.solution:
The distance from home decreases by 60 m. The time increases by 7 minutes.

Use the positive change in distance travelled divided by the time: \(\frac{60}{7}\).

The answer is \(\frac{60}{7}\).

blocks.html: Speed is non-negative even when the distance-from-home graph has a negative slope.

blocks.solution:
The distance from home decreases by 64 m. The time increases by 11 minutes.

Use the positive change in distance travelled divided by the time: \(\frac{64}{11}\).

The answer is \(\frac{64}{11}\).

sections.title: What distance should I use for a whole journey?
sections.label: Average
sections.intro: Add the lengths of the parts that were travelled. A trip out and back can start and finish at the same place while still covering a distance.

blocks.html: Divide total distance travelled by the total time, including any stops.

blocks.prompt:
Time from start (min)Distance from home (m)
00
525
1225
200

The graph starts at home and ends at home. Find the average speed for the whole trip in metres per minute. Give your answer exactly.

field.label: Average speed in metres per minute

blocks.hint: Use the complete distance travelled, even when the final distance from home is zero.
blocks.solution:
The outgoing leg is 25 m and the return leg is also 25 m, giving 50 m in total.

Divide by the whole time, including the stop: \(\frac{5}{2}\).

The answer is \(\frac{5}{2}\).

retry.feedback: The final distance from home is zero, but the traveller moved out and came back.

igcse-0580-practical-graphs-straight-rat.description: Use a change triangle to find and compare rates on graphs with units.

sections.title: Why do the differences matter?
sections.label: Rate
sections.intro: Choose two clear points on the straight segment. Form a change triangle with a horizontal run and vertical rise.

blocks.html: Gradient is vertical change divided by horizontal change.

figure.alt: Volume increases from 8 litres with a change triangle.
figure.caption: From one to three hours, the tank gains 8 litres, so the rate is 4 litres per hour.

blocks.prompt:
Time (h)Volume (L)
359
698

The table gives two points on a straight filling graph. Find the increase in volume per hour.
blocks.hint: A rate is a change in one quantity per unit of the other quantity.
blocks.solution:
The volume rises by 39 L during 3 hours.

Divide the change in volume by the change in time: \(13\).

The answer is \(13\).

blocks.html: Measure both changes in the units on the axes.

The table gives two points on a straight filling graph. Find the increase in volume per hour.
blocks.hint: A rate is a change in one quantity per unit of the other quantity.

Divide the change in volume by the change in time: \(4\).

The answer is \(4\).

sections.title: How do I use a rate to predict a change?
sections.label: Change
sections.intro: When the rate stays constant, each extra hour adds the same amount. Multiply the gradient by the time interval to find the change.

blocks.html: The starting amount belongs to the total. The rate tells you how much is added over another interval.

blocks.prompt:
Time (h)Volume (L)

The straight graph is continued at the same rate for 5 hours. How much extra liquid will enter during those hours?
blocks.hint: Find the rate first, then multiply by the new time interval.
blocks.solution:
The rate from the two points is 56 L in 4 hours, which is 14 L per hour.

Multiply the rate by 5 hours.

The answer is \(70\).

blocks.html: If a question asks for extra volume, keep it separate from the total volume.

blocks.solution:
The rate from the two points is 40 L in 8 hours, which is 5 L per hour.

Multiply the rate by 9 hours.

The answer is \(45\).

sections.title: How can I compare two rates fairly?
sections.label: Compare
sections.intro: Work out both rates in matching units. Then compare how much changes in one unit of time or distance.

blocks.html: The steeper line corresponds to the bigger rate when axes have the same scales.

blocks.hint: The heights on the graph represent volumes, not rates.
blocks.solution:
Use the two points to find the rate of the first tank: \(15\) L per hour.

Compare the two rates after writing them in the same units.

The answer is \(4\).

sections.intro: Vertical change on a speed–time graph is change in speed. Dividing that change by time gives acceleration.

igcse-0580-practical-graphs-tangents.description: Place a tangent at the requested point and use its slope as the rate at that point.

sections.title: Which line should I use on a curved graph?
sections.label: Touch
sections.intro: Draw a straight line whose direction matches the curve at the requested point. Choose two readable points on the tangent line.

blocks.html: Use a wide triangle on the tangent to reduce the effect of small reading errors.

figure.alt: Curve and dashed tangent touching at time 4 and volume 12.
figure.caption: The dashed tangent and the curve have the same direction at the marked point.

blocks.prompt: A volume–time curve has a tangent drawn. Two readable points on that same tangent are \((11,22)\) and \((13,44)\). Time is in minutes and volume is in litres. Estimate the filling rate in litres per minute.

field.label: Filling rate in litres per minute

blocks.hint: Use the straight tangent line, even though the original graph is curved.
blocks.solution:
The two points on the tangent differ by 22 L and 2 minutes.

The tangent's gradient is \(11\). This estimates the rate at the point of contact.

The answer is \(11\).

blocks.html: The two points used for the gradient lie on the tangent. They need not lie on the curve.

blocks.hint: Use the straight tangent line, even though the original graph is curved.

The answer is \(15\).

sections.title: How do I explain a falling tangent?
sections.label: Fall
sections.intro: A tangent falls from left to right when the vertical quantity is decreasing. The gradient carries a minus sign.

blocks.html: Give a signed gradient for rate of change. Give a positive magnitude when asked how much is lost per unit.

blocks.prompt: At one time the tangent of a temperature–time graph passes through \((12,59)\) and \((15,23)\). Time is in minutes and temperature is in degrees Celsius. Estimate the decrease in temperature per minute.

field.label: Cooling rate in degrees Celsius per minute

blocks.hint: A falling tangent has a negative gradient. A question about the amount of decrease calls for the magnitude.
blocks.solution:
The temperature goes down by 36 degrees while time goes up by 3 minutes.

The gradient is negative. The decrease per minute is its positive magnitude, \(12\).

The answer is \(12\).

blocks.html: Read the units before comparing the values.

blocks.prompt: At one time the tangent of a temperature–time graph passes through \((5,139)\) and \((12,27)\). Time is in minutes and temperature is in degrees Celsius. Estimate the decrease in temperature per minute.

sections.title: How do I describe changes in steepness?
sections.label: Range
sections.intro: Compare the gradient estimates at the requested points. A larger positive slope means the quantity is growing faster if the axes use the same units.

blocks.html: A high graph value can have a shallow slope. Use the tangent for the rate.

blocks.prompt: At two points of a filling curve the tangent slopes are 13 and 17 litres per minute. By how much does the greater rate exceed the smaller rate?
blocks.hint: Compare the slopes of the tangents. The position on the graph does not tell you the rate.
blocks.solution:
The larger slope belongs to the greater filling rate.

Subtract 13 from 17.

The answer is \(4\).
